Mexican Fisheries Firm Mar Profundo Enters Insolvency, Operations Disrupted

MEXICO CITY, June 12 — Mar Profundo S.A. de C.V., one of Mexico’s largest fisheries companies, has entered insolvency proceedings, disrupting its fishing and processing operations along the country’s Pacific coast, company officials and industry representatives said Wednesday.

The insolvency filing, made Tuesday in a district court in Mazatlán, Sinaloa, follows several quarters of mounting financial pressure, according to a statement from Mar Profundo’s board of directors. The company, which operates a fleet of 34 vessels and two processing plants, cited “continued market volatility and increased operational costs” as key factors behind its decision.

“After exhausting all other options to stabilize the business, we have initiated court-supervised insolvency to seek protection from creditors while we work on a plan to restructure our obligations,” said CEO Ernesto Paredes in a written statement. “Our immediate priority is to maintain the safety of our employees and vessels while we assess which parts of our operations can continue during this process.”

As of Wednesday, Mar Profundo had suspended all fishing trips scheduled from its Mazatlán and Ensenada bases. The company’s two plants, which process tuna, sardine, and shrimp, are operating at reduced capacity, with only essential staff on site, according to union representatives.

“We were told this morning to stay home until further notice,” said María López, a plant worker in Mazatlán. “Many of us are worried about when — or if — we will be called back.”

The National Fisheries Confederation confirmed that Mar Profundo’s vessels are currently docked, pending the outcome of the court’s review. “This is a major shock for the sector,” said confederation president Guillermo Torres. “Mar Profundo is responsible for a significant share of landings in the Pacific region. The immediate freeze on their activities is causing uncertainty among crews and plant workers.”

Industry analysts estimate Mar Profundo accounted for close to 12% of Mexico’s total fisheries production last year. The company is also a major employer in Sinaloa and Baja California, regions heavily dependent on fisheries for local jobs.

A court hearing has been scheduled for June 19 to determine the next steps in the insolvency process. Sources familiar with the proceedings said the company’s management is seeking to negotiate with creditors and explore options for partial resumption of fishing trips if interim funding can be secured.

“There is still a path forward, but it will depend on successful negotiations,” said fisheries analyst Sofía Méndez. “For now, the immediate effect is a halt in most of Mar Profundo’s operations.”
